gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the 4Patriots 2200X manual lists 1,200 W of solar input (600 W × 2 Anderson ports, 12–59 V DC), which is more than the 1,000 W on the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 or EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max, or that its '4,000 cycles' is measured at 80% depth of discharge rather than down to 80% of original capacity, so it cannot be compared with rivals' cycle ratings.
standout_why: I compared against the cited powerstationgearlab.com (2200X 'doesn't publish a maximum solar input'; end-of-life threshold 'Not stated'), solar-home.space (solar input 'Not listed'; 2200X cycles 'end percentage not stated'; Elite 200 V2 '3,900 W (resistive loads)' with no cycle end point) and powerstations.reviews (2200X max solar 'not stated', end point 'not stated'; it lists each brand's cycle count as given, without adjusting for different end points). solargenadvisor.com and unpluggedwatts.com could not be opened because of certificate errors. Our own current page also says 'max solar input not published'. None of these pages read the 4Patriots manual. None notes that the 2200X cycle figure uses a depth-of-discharge condition, or that BLUETTI's 3,900 W is a mode for resistive loads only, not a motor-start surge.
decides: This confirms the pick (Elite 200 V2 or DELTA 2 Max over the 2200X) and changes the reason. Solar input is not a 2200X weakness: it accepts 1,200 W, more than both alternatives. The real weakness is the small panel in the bundle, which the manual rates at 28–30 h to charge from one 100 W panel. That leaves price ($3,199 vs $1,199 for the same 200 W panel bundle, $1.43 vs $0.58 per Wh), the 1-year vs 5-year warranty, and the 1,500 W vs 1,800 W AC input as the differences that hold up. ChatGPT's 'solar charging transparency' con and our page's 'not published' cell should both be dropped. In the output column, '2,200 W (4,400 W surge, 0.5 s)' and '2,600 W (3,900 W lifting)' are different kinds of figure: BLUETTI's 3,900 W covers resistive loads only, and BLUETTI's US, CA and UK pages give no motor-start surge. The table needs a footnote saying so.

findings.label: Solar input
findings.value: 600 W × 2 (1,200 W total), Anderson-compatible solar/DC ports, 12–59 V DC
findings.note: Maker's manual hosted on ManualsLib: 'Solar input 600 W x 2' on p. 27, DC input voltage 12–59 V on p. 12. The 1,200 W total assumes both ports run at once; the manual excerpt does not say whether they can be combined.

findings.label: Cycle life as rated
findings.value: more than 4,000 cycles at 80% depth of discharge; end-of-life capacity not stated
findings.note: Manual p. 26: 'More than 4000 cycles, down to 80% DoD'. DoD is how much of the battery each cycle uses, not how much capacity is left at end of life. EcoFlow and BLUETTI quote cycles until the battery holds 80% of its original capacity, so the figures are not like for like.

findings.label: Surge, AC input, solar charge time, warranty, weight
findings.value: 4,400 W for 0.5 s; AC input 1,500 W max (about 1.5 h); 28–30 h on one 100 W panel; 1-year warranty (0–365 days from delivery); 57.5 lb

findings.label: Price
findings.source_title: Portable Solar Generators | Silent Backup Power Solutions – 4Patriots

findings.label: Lifting power vs surge
findings.value: 2,600 W rated; 3,900 W Power Lifting for pure resistive loads only; no motor-start surge figure published
findings.note: Maker's wording: 'supports pure resistive loads of up to 3,900W'. The US and UK maker pages use the same wording and give no separate surge figure. This is not comparable with the 2200X's 4,400 W/0.5 s surge.

findings.label: Solar and AC input
findings.value: PV 12–60 V / 20 A, 1,000 W max; AC input 1,800 W
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 Portable Power Station | 2,600W 2,080Wh
findings.note: From the maker's FAQ. The 2200X takes 200 W more solar but 300 W less AC input.

findings.label: Price
findings.note: Checked with storecheck on bluettipower.com. Per Wh: $1,199 ÷ 2,073.6 Wh = $0.58; $899 ÷ 2,073.6 Wh = $0.43. The US page title says 2,080 Wh but its FAQ says 2,073.6 Wh; I used 2,073.6.

findings.label: Cycle life (reviewer's table)
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 portable power station review (The Gadgeteer, Greg Cleveland)
findings.note: Greg Cleveland's spec table says '6000+ (80%)'; the table is not attributed to BLUETTI. The same table lists 'Max Surge Power 3900W', which conflicts with BLUETTI's own resistive-only wording.

findings.label: Cycle life, solar input, warranty, price
findings.value: 3,000+ cycles until 80% of original capacity; up to 1,000 W solar; 5-year warranty; $1,029
findings.source_title: EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max Portable Power Station | EcoFlow US
findings.note: Maker's wording: '10 years of daily use until hitting 80% of its original capacity… 3000+ cycles'. Per Wh: $1,029 ÷ 2,048 Wh = $0.50. X-Boost reaches 3,400 W but, like BLUETTI's lifting mode, it is not a surge rating.
